title: Temporal and the services on inf

story: Five weeks into the pilot, a teammate asks in Slack: "Did Nova really run twice on RH-1234 in September? And is the CI fixer working on anything right now?" You open the Temporal UI, the web page of Temporal, the workflow engine that records every step of every agent run. There are hundreds of runs. Their workflow IDs, the names we give runs, such as nova:RH-1234, help a little, but you cannot ask for "every run that touched RH-1234" or "every running CI-fixer run" if the name does not say it.

And September is simply not there. Closed runs disappear after a while, and nobody chose how long that while is. Both problems were decided, without anyone noticing, on the day our Temporal was installed.
hook.question: What must we decide when we install our own Temporal, so that we can still find any run we need, weeks later?

p: The product already runs a Temporal for its own workflows, and our agents do not share it. An agent platform has storms of its own, such as forty red builds in ten minutes, and gets upgraded on its own schedule. If it shared the product's Temporal, a mistake on our side could slow down or break customer workflows. So the platform gets a small Temporal of its own on inf, our Kubernetes cluster for internal tools.

A Temporal server is a set of services in front of a database. Every event of every run, each step, timer and signal, is a row in that database, here a small Postgres on AWS RDS (the AWS service that runs databases for you). The password for that database lives in Vault, our secret store, and reaches the server through an ExternalSecret, and the server itself is the official Temporal Helm chart installed by our infrastructure code, as for any service on inf.

deeper.h: Go deeper: one number you can never change
p: Temporal splits the work of keeping histories into history shards, and every run belongs to exactly one shard for its whole life. The number of shards is chosen at the first install and can never change afterwards, because changing it would move every run. Ours is 128, the same as the product's Temporal, which is plenty for a small platform. If you install a test copy with a different number, you cannot later point it at the real database.

Other settings are small on purpose: a db.t4g.small database with deletion protection and 14 days of backups, a few database connections per service, and the web UI reachable only from the VPN or Teleport, our tool for reaching internal systems. Inside the cluster a NetworkPolicy lets only pods in the ai-agents namespace reach Temporal's port 7233.

read.h: A namespace is where the rules live
p: Inside one Temporal server, a namespace is a separate space for a group of workflows. Workflow IDs are unique per namespace, permissions can be set per namespace, and so can the two settings from the story. Ours is called ai-agents.

The first setting is retention: how long Temporal keeps a run after it has closed. Until then you can open its full history in the UI, replay it in a test, and Temporal still remembers its ID, which matters for the CI fixer's rule that a returning root cause goes to a person. After retention the run is deleted. The command-line default is 3 days; ours is 30 days, long enough for a weekly review and a monthly look back.

code.file: your terminal (temporal CLI, dev server running)
code.text:
temporal operator namespace create --namespace ai-agents --retention 720h
temporal operator namespace describe --namespace ai-agents

notes.text: 720 hours is 30 days. Without --retention the CLI uses 72 hours.

read.see:
Namespace ai-agents successfully registered.
  NamespaceInfo.State                   Registered
  Config.WorkflowExecutionRetentionTtl  720h0m0s

read.h: Search attributes: fields you can ask about
p: The second setting answers the first question in the story. A search attribute is a named field that a run carries and that you can filter on, in the UI or with temporal workflow list --query. Temporal has a few built in, such as WorkflowType and ExecutionStatus. Our own fields must be registered in the namespace before any run uses them: Agent (nova, cifix and so on), JiraKey (the ticket) and RunKind (ticket, routine or schedule). All three are Keyword, which means an exact value, compared as a whole, the right type for IDs.

Each run then carries its values from the moment it starts, because the orchestrator, the Temporal worker that starts every run, sets them in its one start function. A run started with a field that the namespace does not know is refused, so a typo fails loudly on the first run instead of quietly making runs unsearchable.

code.text:
temporal operator search-attribute create --namespace ai-agents --name JiraKey --type Keyword
temporal workflow start --namespace ai-agents --type ticketToPr --task-queue ai-agents-nova \
  --workflow-id nova:RH-1234 --search-attribute 'Agent="nova"' --search-attribute 'JiraKey="RH-1234"'
temporal workflow list --namespace ai-agents --query 'JiraKey="RH-1234"'

notes.text: Register the field once per namespace. Agent and RunKind are registered the same way.
Values are JSON, so a string is in double quotes inside the single quotes.
The question from the story, as a query.

read.see:
Status    WorkflowId      Type       StartTime
  Running  nova:RH-1234  ticketToPr  2 seconds ago

$ temporal workflow list --namespace ai-agents --query 'Ticket="RH-1234"'
Error: failed listing workflows: invalid query: invalid search attribute: Ticket

deeper.h: Go deeper: the services that live next to Temporal
p: Three of our services run on inf next to Temporal, in the same ai-agents Kubernetes namespace: the orchestrator worker (two copies), the broker, the service that holds our GitHub, Jira and Slack keys (two copies), and the Slack app (one). They share one small Helm chart with the LLM gateway, the service that adds our Anthropic key to every model call. Their keys come from Vault through ExternalSecrets, their images are pinned by digest, and they run as non-root on a read-only filesystem.

The orchestrator needs to start, stop and tag VMs in the ai-agents AWS account, so its pod gets an AWS role through IRSA, which lets a Kubernetes service account wear an AWS role without a stored key. The sandbox VMs in the other account reach exactly three ports here through PrivateLink, a private path between the two accounts: the broker's sandbox port, the gateway and the telemetry collector. Temporal is not one of them, so a VM can never start or signal a run.

lab.title: A namespace you can search
lab.goal: Create the ai-agents namespace with 30-day retention and our three search attributes, start two runs that carry them, and find each run by ticket and by agent.

guess.q: You start a run with --search-attribute 'Ticket="RH-9"', but the namespace has no attribute called Ticket. What happens?

options.text: Temporal creates the attribute for you.
options.why: Search attributes are part of the namespace's setup. Temporal never invents one from a start call.

options.text: The run starts, and the field is quietly dropped.
options.why: That would make runs unsearchable without anyone noticing. Temporal refuses instead.

options.text: The start is refused, because the namespace has no mapping for Ticket.
options.why: Every custom field must be registered first, so a typo fails on the first run.

follow.say: Start a local Temporal in the first tab and leave it running. It keeps everything in memory.
follow.see:
Temporal Server:      localhost:7233
Temporal UI:          http://localhost:8233

follow.say: In the second tab, create our namespace with 30 days of retention, and read its settings back.
follow.do:
temporal operator namespace create --namespace ai-agents --retention 720h
temporal operator namespace describe --namespace ai-agents | grep -E 'State|Retention'
follow.see:
Namespace ai-agents successfully registered.
  NamespaceInfo.State                   Registered
  Config.WorkflowExecutionRetentionTtl  720h0m0s

follow.say: Register our three fields, all of type Keyword.
follow.do: for sa in Agent JiraKey RunKind; do temporal operator search-attribute create --namespace ai-agents --name $sa --type Keyword; done
follow.see:
Search attributes have been added
Search attributes have been added
Search attributes have been added

follow.say: Start one Nova run and one CI-fixer run, each with its fields. No worker is needed: the runs simply wait.
follow.do:
temporal workflow start --namespace ai-agents --type ticketToPr --task-queue ai-agents-nova --workflow-id nova:RH-1234 \
  --search-attribute 'Agent="nova"' --search-attribute 'JiraKey="RH-1234"' --search-attribute 'RunKind="ticket"'
temporal workflow start --namespace ai-agents --type routineRun --task-queue ai-agents-cifix --workflow-id cifix:fcp:3fa91c27d0e4 \
  --search-attribute 'Agent="cifix"' --search-attribute 'RunKind="routine"'
follow.see:
Running execution:
  WorkflowId  nova:RH-1234
  Type        ticketToPr
  Namespace   ai-agents
  TaskQueue   ai-agents-nova
(and the same block for cifix:fcp:3fa91c27d0e4)

follow.say: Ask the two questions from the story.
follow.do:
temporal workflow list --namespace ai-agents --query 'JiraKey="RH-1234"'
temporal workflow list --namespace ai-agents --query 'Agent="cifix" AND ExecutionStatus="Running"'
follow.see:
Status    WorkflowId      Type       StartTime
  Running  nova:RH-1234  ticketToPr  2 seconds ago
  Status         WorkflowId           Type       StartTime
  Running  cifix:fcp:3fa91c27d0e4  routineRun  2 seconds ago

follow.say: Now make the typo from the guess, at start time.
follow.do: temporal workflow start --namespace ai-agents --type ticketToPr --task-queue ai-agents-nova --workflow-id nova:RH-9 --search-attribute 'Ticket="RH-9"'
follow.see: Error: failed starting workflow: Namespace ai-agents has no mapping defined for search attribute Ticket

lab.build: Open the UI at http://localhost:8233, switch to the ai-agents namespace, and type the same two queries into the search box. Then start a second Nova run, nova:RH-1240, for a different ticket, and write one query that lists every Nova run that is still running, and another that lists every run of kind ticket for RH-1240 only.
checks: namespace describe shows Retention 720h0m0s for ai-agents.
temporal operator search-attribute list --namespace ai-agents shows Agent, JiraKey and RunKind as Keyword.
The JiraKey query returns only nova:RH-1234, and the Agent query returns only the CI-fixer run.
A start with an unregistered field is refused with "no mapping defined".
The UI's search box accepts the same queries as the CLI.
You stopped the dev server with Ctrl+C.

solution.text:
temporal workflow start --namespace ai-agents --type ticketToPr --task-queue ai-agents-nova --workflow-id nova:RH-1240 \
  --search-attribute 'Agent="nova"' --search-attribute 'JiraKey="RH-1240"' --search-attribute 'RunKind="ticket"'
temporal workflow list --namespace ai-agents --query 'Agent="nova" AND ExecutionStatus="Running"'
#   Running  nova:RH-1240  ticketToPr ...
#   Running  nova:RH-1234  ticketToPr ...
temporal workflow list --namespace ai-agents --query 'RunKind="ticket" AND JiraKey="RH-1240"'
#   Running  nova:RH-1240  ticketToPr ...

lab.fix: A teammate's install script registered the ticket field as Text instead of Keyword. Recreate it in a fresh dev server (temporal operator search-attribute create --name JiraKey --type Text), start nova:RH-1234 and nova:RH-12 with their JiraKey values, and query JiraKey="RH". Both runs come back, although neither ticket is called RH: a Text field is split into words and matched like a search engine. Explain why an ID belongs in a Keyword field, where JiraKey="RH" finds nothing, and recreate the field with the right type.
explain: Why does the agent platform have its own Temporal instead of a namespace in the product's?
What does a 30-day retention mean for a run that closed 40 days ago, in the UI and for the CI fixer's "refuse a returning root cause" rule?
Why must search attributes be registered before the first run, and why Keyword for JiraKey?
lab.done: Your ai-agents namespace keeps closed runs for 30 days, knows Agent, JiraKey and RunKind, and finds each run by ticket or by agent.

check.q: The orchestrator starts a run with the search attribute JiraKey, but the namespace was created without registering it. What happens?

options.text: The start is refused because the namespace has no mapping for JiraKey
options.why: Custom fields must exist in the namespace first, so the mistake shows on the first run, not weeks later.

options.text: The run starts and the field is stored as plain text
options.why: Temporal does not guess types or create fields from a start call.

options.text: The run starts, but the field only appears after the run closes
options.why: Fields are set at start and searchable while the run is open. An unknown field is refused at start.

check.q: Our namespace keeps closed runs for 30 days. A CI-fixer run closed 40 days ago. What is true now?

options.text: Its history is still in the UI, because Temporal never deletes histories
options.why: Retention exists exactly to delete closed runs, so the database does not grow forever.

options.text: It is archived to S3 automatically
options.why: Archival is a separate feature that we did not turn on.

options.text: It is gone: the UI cannot show it, and Temporal no longer remembers its ID
options.why: After retention a closed run is deleted, including the memory of its ID that a reuse policy like REJECT_DUPLICATE relies on.

check.q: Why does the agent platform run its own small Temporal instead of a namespace in the product's Temporal?

options.text: The product's Temporal cannot store search attributes
options.why: It can, and it already does. The reason is isolation, not features.

options.text: So agent storms, upgrades and mistakes can never slow or break the product's workflows
options.why: A namespace separates names and settings, but the server, its database and its upgrades would still be shared.

options.text: Because a second Temporal is cheaper than a namespace
options.why: A namespace costs almost nothing. A second server costs a database and a few pods, a price paid for isolation.

p: Temporal for the agents runs on inf-rhinohealth, set up like n8n: multi_tenant/accounts/infrastructure/ai-agents/ai-agents.hcl and the units temporal/{secrets,sg,rds,repository}. The secrets unit generates the database password into Vault at infrastructure/ai-agents/temporal; rds is terraform-aws-modules/rds 6.12.0, db.t4g.small, deletion protection, 14-day backups, Postgres 17 unless Temporal 1.31 is confirmed on 18 (Andy, who knows our Temporal setup, reviews). modules/ai-agents-temporal creates the Kubernetes namespace, the ExternalSecret from vault-store and a helm_release of chart temporal 1.5.0, starting from the product's values: numHistoryShards 128, namespace ai-agents with 30-day retention.

A post-install Job registers Agent, JiraKey and RunKind as Keyword; G5 adds Routine, RoutineOutcome and Stage, G1 adds Step and HarnessVersion. The UI is temporal-ai-agents.example.com on envoy-internal (VPN or Teleport only), a NetworkPolicy keeps port 7233 to the ai-agents namespace, and a VMServiceScrape collects its metrics. The orchestrator worker, broker and Slack app are helm_release units through modules/ai-agents-service, with ExternalSecrets, IRSA into the ai-agents account and a PrivateLink NLB that exposes only the broker's sandbox port, the gateway and the OTel collector.

tickets.why: Our own Temporal: RDS, the Vault secret, the Helm release, the ai-agents namespace with retention and search attributes.
The orchestrator worker, broker and Slack app on inf, their secrets and roles, and the PrivateLink path for sandboxes.

words.plain: A separate space inside one Temporal server, with its own workflow IDs and its own settings.
How long a closed run is kept before Temporal deletes it. Ours is 30 days.
A named field on a run that you can filter on, such as JiraKey. Custom ones must be registered first.
A search attribute type for exact values compared as a whole, right for IDs like RH-1234.
A slice of Temporal's storage; the number is fixed at the first install and can never change.

review.q: Write the two commands that give a fresh namespace our retention and our ticket field.
review.a: temporal operator namespace create --namespace ai-agents --retention 720h, and temporal operator search-attribute create --namespace ai-agents --name JiraKey --type Keyword (and the same for Agent and RunKind).

review.q: Someone asks for every running CI-fixer run. Write the query and say what makes it possible.
review.a: Agent="cifix" AND ExecutionStatus="Running". It works because Agent is registered in the namespace and every run sets it at start.

remember: Install our own Temporal once and decide its namespace well: 30 days of retention, and the fields Agent, JiraKey and RunKind registered before the first run, so any run can be found later.
